B.1: Open enrollment ends on December seventh, and one choice you make this fall can be very hard to undo. It is the choice between Medicare Advantage and a Medigap plan. Medicare itself warns that in most cases, if you drop a Medigap policy to join an Advantage plan, you may not be able to get it back, and in some cases you may not be able to get any Medigap policy at all. Here is what the official rules say.
B.2: Meet Carol and Ben. Carol turns sixty-five this spring, and she is about to choose her very first Medicare coverage. Ben is sixty-eight. He has a Medicare Advantage plan, and he is wondering whether to return to Original Medicare and add a Medigap plan. Both of them are about to meet rules that most people only learn after it is too late.
B.3: Every fact in this video comes from official sources: the government guide called Choosing a Medigap Policy, written by Medicare and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, plus the Medicare website and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. No sales pages, and no insurance agents. First, what Medigap actually is.
B.4: Medigap, officially called Medicare Supplement Insurance, is extra insurance that you buy from a private company. Original Medicare, which is Part A and Part B, covers hospital and doctor costs, but you still owe deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. Medigap helps pay your share of those costs. And Medicare itself does not pay anything toward the cost of buying a Medigap policy.
B.5: Medigap plans are standardized. In most states they are named by letters: A, B, C, D, F, G, K, L, M and N. All plans with the same letter offer the same basic benefits, no matter which company sells them. Massachusetts, Minnesota and Wisconsin are the exceptions. The only difference between two Plan G policies is the price, so compare Plan G with Plan G, not with Plan N.
B.6: Let us look at Plan G. It covers Part A coinsurance and hospital costs, up to an additional three hundred sixty-five days after Medicare benefits are used. It covers Part B coinsurance or copayment, the first three pints of blood, hospice coinsurance, skilled nursing facility coinsurance, the Part A deductible, and Part B excess charges. Foreign travel emergency care is covered at eighty percent.
B.7: Now what Plan G does not cover: the Part B deductible, which is two hundred eighty-three dollars in twenty twenty-six. Medigap plans sold to people who are new to Medicare on or after January first, twenty twenty, are not allowed to cover that deductible. That is why Plans C and F are closed to new people, and Plans D and G are the ones they can buy instead.
B.8: Medigap also leaves some things out. It generally does not cover long-term care, like non-skilled care in a nursing home, vision or dental care, hearing aids, glasses, or private-duty nursing. Medigap plans sold after two thousand five do not include prescription drugs, so for drugs you need a separate Part D plan. And one policy covers only one person, so spouses each need their own.
B.9: What does it cost? You pay the private company a separate monthly premium for your Medigap policy, on top of the monthly Part B premium you pay to Medicare. In twenty twenty-six, the standard Part B premium is two hundred two dollars and ninety cents. And the premium for the same plan letter can be very different from one company to another, so Medicare says to get quotes from more than one.
B.10: There is a second price trap: how the company sets the price. Medicare describes three ways. Community-rated generally means the same premium for everyone, whatever their age. Issue-age-rated means your price depends on your age when you buy, and does not rise because you get older. Attained-age-rated means your price rises as you age. In Medicare's own example, which it says is not an actual price, one hundred twenty dollars at sixty-five becomes one hundred twenty-six at sixty-six.
B.11: Now the most important rule: the Medigap Open Enrollment Period. It lasts six months, and it starts the first month you have Part B and you are sixty-five or older. It is a one-time period, and it does not repeat every year. During it, a company cannot refuse to sell you any policy it offers, cannot use medical underwriting, and cannot charge you more because of your health problems.
B.12: Outside that window, the rules change. Medicare says you may pay more, you may have fewer plans to choose from, and there is no guarantee that a company will sell you a policy if you do not meet its medical underwriting rules. This matters for Carol. If her Part B starts the month she turns sixty-five, her six months start then, and Medicare says they cannot be changed or repeated.
B.13: Now Ben. He wants to leave Medicare Advantage and buy a Medigap plan. Medicare says it is illegal to sell a Medigap policy to someone in an Advantage plan, unless that person is switching back to Original Medicare. And if Ben is not in his open enrollment period and has no guaranteed issue right, a company may deny him a policy, or charge him more, because of his health.
B.14: But there are situations where Ben is protected. Medicare calls them guaranteed issue rights. One example is when his Advantage plan leaves Medicare or stops giving care in his area, or when he moves out of its service area. Then the company must sell him a policy, must cover his pre-existing conditions, and cannot charge him more for his health. He must apply no more than sixty-three days after his Advantage coverage ends. His state may give him even more rights.
B.15: There is also a trial right. If you joined an Advantage plan when you were first eligible for Part A at sixty-five, and within the first year you choose to go back to Original Medicare, you can buy any Medigap policy sold in your state. If you dropped a Medigap policy to try Advantage for the first time, and you have been in the plan less than a year, you can ask for your old policy back, if the same company still sells it.
B.16: So what should you do this fall? One: before you drop any Medigap policy, remember that Medicare says you may not get it back. Two: before you call a company, find out whether you are in your open enrollment period or have a guaranteed issue right. Three: compare the same plan letter from more than one company, and ask how the price is set. Four: call your State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which gives free help and is not connected to any insurance company.
B.17: To sum up, five facts. One: Medigap pays your share of Original Medicare costs, and it is sold by private companies. Two: Plan G covers a lot, but not the Part B deductible. Three: your Medigap open enrollment lasts six months, and it happens only once. Four: after it, a company may deny you or charge you more, unless you have a guaranteed issue right. Five: if you drop Medigap for Advantage, you may not get it back.
B.18: If this helped, send it to someone who is about to turn sixty-five, and tell me in the comments which plan you were thinking about. One last thing: this video is general information, not insurance advice. Rules, prices and plans differ by state, so confirm with Medicare or your State Insurance Department before you act.
